The Mail Room/Lesson 21/Lesson text (draft)

Online Learning

Lesson text (draft) · Teacher's sheet

The spammers are watching

Lesson 20 ended with the triangle filter, certificate and all, losing ground the very next morning. Look closer at what the spammers do now. They no longer send a big batch of junk and wait. They send one message, see whether it got through, and then decide what to send next. If “FREE” in the subject gets caught, the next message says “F.R.E.E”. If the filter lets a message with a link through, the next hundred all have links. Every decision the filter makes is information for them, and they use it straight away.

Your monitoring shows the damage. The filter is retrained every night on the day’s labelled mail, and every morning it starts losing again, because whatever it learned overnight is exactly what the spammers stop doing. The mail today depends on what the filter did yesterday, and on what it did five minutes ago. Every guarantee from lessons 2 to 20 began with one promise: the messages are drawn independently from one fixed distribution D\mathcal DD, and the learner gets a whole training sequence S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm before it has to say anything. An opponent who reacts to you is about as far from that promise as anything can be, so not one of those guarantees applies.

So what can a learner promise when the mail is chosen by someone who reads its decisions? It sounds hopeless. It is not, and this lesson is about what you can still prove.

One message at a time

First, the shape of the new problem. Messages arrive one at a time. For each one, the filter must decide on the spot, junk or keep. Only afterwards does it find out the right answer, because a user opens the message and either reports it as junk or doesn’t. Then the next message arrives.

Each pass through that loop is a round. On round ttt:

  1. a message xtx_txt​ arrives (the spammers chose it);
  2. the learner announces a prediction ptp_tpt​, its label for xtx_txt​, with 1 for junk and 0 for keep, as always;
  3. the true label yty_tyt​ is revealed;
  4. the learner may update itself before round t+1t + 1t+1.

A learner that works this way is an online learner, and the setting is online learning. Lesson 1 named it, with the stockbroker who must decide every day using only what happened so far; now we study it. There is no separate training phase and test phase. Every message is first a test (the learner must predict) and then a training example (the learner sees the label). The score is the number of mistakes, the rounds where pt≠ytp_t \neq y_tpt​=yt​. Each mistake is a junk message in someone’s inbox or a real message in the junk folder, so the filter is paying for its education as it goes.

[diagram:protocol: built on the lesson page]

Notice what is missing: no D\mathcal DD. We make no assumption about where the messages come from. They may be fixed in advance, random, or chosen by an opponent who watches the learner’s every move and changes tactics after each decision. We call that opponent the adversary. A guarantee that holds against the adversary holds against anything, which is exactly what a filter facing real spammers needs.

Can anything be guaranteed against such an opponent? Let’s try the simplest possible attack before anything else. The adversary sends the same message every round, waits for the prediction, and then declares the opposite label to be the true one. Whatever the learner does, it is wrong.

def learner(history, x):
    past = [y for (u, y) in history if u == x]
    return int(2 * sum(past) >= len(past)) if past else 0

history, mistakes, T = [], 0, 100
for t in range(T):
    x = (1, 0, 1, 1)
    p = learner(history, x)
    y = 1 - p
    mistakes += p != y
    history.append((x, y))
print(mistakes, "mistakes in", T, "rounds")

It prints 100 mistakes in 100 rounds. The learner here is a sensible one: it predicts whatever label message xxx got most often in the past. It does not matter. The adversary reads p and sets y = 1 - p, so every round is a mistake. Replace learner with anything you like that returns 0 or 1, and the count stays at 100.

So with no restriction at all, the adversary wins every round. To say anything, we have to restrict the adversary somehow, the same way lesson 1 had to restrict the learner. The question is which restriction is both realistic and enough.

Realizability buys a mistake bound

The attack above works because the adversary’s labels make no sense: the same message is junk on Monday and keep on Tuesday. Real junk has a rule behind it. So here is the first restriction, and you have met it before. In lesson 2 it was called realizability: the labels come from some hypothesis in a class H\mathcal HH that the learner knows in advance.

Online, it reads like this. Before the game starts, the learner is told H\mathcal HH. The adversary still chooses every message, and in whatever order and with whatever cunning it likes. It may even put off deciding which hypothesis is “the truth” until the end, as long as, at the end, some single h⋆∈Hh^\star \in \mathcal Hh⋆∈H agrees with every label it gave. So all labels satisfy yt=h⋆(xt)y_t = h^\star(x_t)yt​=h⋆(xt​). Under that rule, the attack with one repeated message dies: once the adversary has called xxx junk, it must call xxx junk forever, because one hypothesis cannot give one message two labels.

Let’s use the smallest class we know, the one-feature class of lesson 1. Messages are four bits FLUN (says “FREE”, has a link, unknown sender, sent at night), and the class has four hypotheses, H1={hF,hL,hU,hN}\mathcal H_1 = \{h_F, h_L, h_U, h_N\}H1​={hF​,hL​,hU​,hN​}, where hFh_FhF​ says junk exactly when the F bit is 1, and so on. The adversary has picked one of the four as the truth, or will pick one by the end. How many mistakes can it force?

That number, the worst the adversary can do, is how we will measure online learners. Here it is in words first: run the learner on a sequence of examples and count its mistakes; then take the worst sequence the adversary could choose, over every length and every h⋆h^\starh⋆ in the class. If that worst count is finite, the learner has a promise to make: “whatever you send me, I will make at most this many mistakes, ever.”

Now the notation. A sequence of TTT labelled messages is written S=((x1,y1),…,(xT,yT))S = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_T, y_T))S=((x1​,y1​),…,(xT​,yT​)), where TTT is the number of rounds. We call SSS realizable by H\mathcal HH when some h⋆∈Hh^\star \in \mathcal Hh⋆∈H has yt=h⋆(xt)y_t = h^\star(x_t)yt​=h⋆(xt​) for every round ttt. For an online learner AAA,

MA(S)=∣{t∈[T]:pt≠yt}∣,MA(H)=sup⁡SMA(S).M_A(S) = \left| \{ t \in [T] : p_t \neq y_t \} \right|, \qquad M_A(\mathcal H) = \sup_{S} M_A(S).MA​(S)=∣{t∈[T]:pt​=yt​}∣,MA​(H)=Ssup​MA​(S).

Read it from the inside out.

  • ptp_tpt​ is the prediction AAA made on round ttt, and yty_tyt​ the label revealed afterwards. The test pt≠ytp_t \neq y_tpt​=yt​ asks one yes/no question: was round ttt a mistake?
  • [T][T][T] is the set of round numbers {1,2,…,T}\{1, 2, \dots, T\}{1,2,…,T}, as [m][m][m] was the set of example positions in lesson 1.
  • The braces {t∈[T]:… }\{ t \in [T] : \dots \}{t∈[T]:…} collect the rounds where the answer is yes. The colon reads “such that”: the rounds ttt such that AAA got round ttt wrong.
  • The bars ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ mean “how many”. So MA(S)M_A(S)MA​(S) is the number of mistakes AAA makes on the sequence SSS. No division this time: online, we count mistakes rather than average them.
  • sup⁡S\sup_SsupS​ (“supremum over SSS”) means: the largest value over every realizable sequence SSS, of any length TTT, labelled by any h⋆∈Hh^\star \in \mathcal Hh⋆∈H. It is a maximum that is allowed to be infinite, or to be approached without being reached.

In plain words: MA(S)M_A(S)MA​(S) is how many mistakes learner AAA makes on one sequence, and MA(H)M_A(\mathcal H)MA​(H) is the most mistakes any adversary can force on it, as long as the labels follow some hypothesis in H\mathcal HH. For a tiny number: if the learner predicts “junk” on every message and the adversary sends 1000, 0100, 0010 (all keep) and then 0001 (junk), labelled by hNh_NhN​, then MA(S)=3M_A(S) = 3MA​(S)=3.

A bound MA(H)≤B<∞M_A(\mathcal H) \le B < \inftyMA​(H)≤B<∞ is a mistake bound (here BBB is just a number, not the norm bound of lessons 12 to 15). A class H\mathcal HH is online learnable if some online learner AAA has a mistake bound for it. For now we ignore running time completely, as lesson 3 did at first with PAC learning: the learners in the first half of this lesson may be slow, and only the last two learners will be efficient.

Consistent: keep the survivors

Lesson 2 taught us a learner that works in the batch world: return any hypothesis that is consistent with every example (under realizability, that is what empirical risk minimization, ERM, returns). The online version is just as natural. Keep the set of hypotheses that have agreed with every label so far; when a message arrives, pick any one of them and predict with it. Call it Consistent.

The set of hypotheses still consistent with everything seen is the version space. On round 1 it is the whole class. After each round, every hypothesis that disagreed with the revealed label leaves.

Let’s play it against the adversary on H1\mathcal H_1H1​. Suppose Consistent picks the first surviving hypothesis in the order F, L, U, N. The adversary knows this (it may know the learner’s code; only the truth is hidden from the learner). Before reading the table, ask yourself what message the adversary should send first, to make hFh_FhF​ wrong.

tmessage FLUNConsistent predicts withprediction ptp_tpt​label yty_tyt​version space after
11000hFh_FhF​10L, U, N
20100hLh_LhL​10U, N
30010hUh_UhU​10N
40001hNh_NhN​11N
51111hNh_NhN​11N
60000hNh_NhN​00N

The trick is to send a message on which only the chosen hypothesis says junk, and then call it keep. Three rounds, three mistakes, each removing exactly one hypothesis. The labels are realizable, by hNh_NhN​, so the adversary played fair. After that, only hNh_NhN​ is left and Consistent never errs again.

Let’s write the version space down. Call it VtV_tVt​, the hypotheses still standing at the start of round ttt. Then V1=HV_1 = \mathcal HV1​=H and

Vt+1={h∈Vt:h(xt)=yt}.V_{t+1} = \{ h \in V_t : h(x_t) = y_t \}.Vt+1​={h∈Vt​:h(xt​)=yt​}.
  • VtV_tVt​ is a set of hypotheses; h∈Vth \in V_th∈Vt​ reads “hhh is one of them”.
  • h(xt)=yth(x_t) = y_th(xt​)=yt​ asks whether hhh agrees with the label just revealed.
  • The braces and colon read “the hypotheses hhh in VtV_tVt​ such that hhh agrees with round ttt”.

In plain words: after each round, keep exactly the hypotheses that got that round right. In the table, V1={hF,hL,hU,hN}V_1 = \{h_F, h_L, h_U, h_N\}V1​={hF​,hL​,hU​,hN​}; round 1 reveals that 1000 is keep, and only hFh_FhF​ says junk on 1000, so V2={hL,hU,hN}V_2 = \{h_L, h_U, h_N\}V2​={hL​,hU​,hN​}. Here is the table again as code, with the version space printed after each round:

H = "FLUN"
h = lambda name, x: int(x[H.index(name)])
consistent = lambda V, x: h(min(V, key=H.index), x)

def play(learn, stream):
    V, M = set(H), 0
    for x, y in stream:
        p = learn(V, x)
        M += p != y
        V = {n for n in V if h(n, x) == y}
        print(x, p, y, "".join(sorted(V, key=H.index)))
    return M

s1 = [("1000", 0), ("0100", 0), ("0010", 0), ("0001", 1),
      ("1111", 1), ("0000", 0)]
print(play(consistent, s1))

It prints the six rows of the table (1000 1 0 LUN, 0100 1 0 UN, 0010 1 0 N, then three rows ending in N) and finally 3, the mistake count MA(S)M_A(S)MA​(S). The line V = {n for n in V if h(n, x) == y} is the version-space formula, symbol for symbol.

Could the adversary have done better than three? Here is the argument that it couldn’t, in words first. Every mistake throws out at least one hypothesis: the one Consistent predicted with was wrong, so it leaves. And the truth h⋆h^\starh⋆ never leaves, because it is never wrong. So the version space starts with ∣H∣|\mathcal H|∣H∣ hypotheses, loses at least one per mistake, and always keeps at least one.

Claim (Consistent’s mistake bound). For a finite class H\mathcal HH, MConsistent(H)≤∣H∣−1M_{\text{Consistent}}(\mathcal H) \le |\mathcal H| - 1MConsistent​(H)≤∣H∣−1.

Proof. Run Consistent on any realizable sequence and let MMM be its number of mistakes. On a mistake round, the hypothesis hhh that Consistent used predicted pt=h(xt)≠ytp_t = h(x_t) \neq y_tpt​=h(xt​)=yt​, so h∉Vt+1h \notin V_{t+1}h∈/Vt+1​: the version space shrinks by at least one. On other rounds it does not grow, since Vt+1⊆VtV_{t+1} \subseteq V_tVt+1​⊆Vt​. So after all TTT rounds, ∣VT+1∣≤∣H∣−M|V_{T+1}| \le |\mathcal H| - M∣VT+1​∣≤∣H∣−M.

The truth h⋆h^\starh⋆ has h⋆(xt)=yth^\star(x_t) = y_th⋆(xt​)=yt​ on every round, so by induction it is in every VtV_tVt​, and ∣VT+1∣≥1|V_{T+1}| \ge 1∣VT+1​∣≥1. Putting the two together, 1≤∣H∣−M1 \le |\mathcal H| - M1≤∣H∣−M, which rearranges to M≤∣H∣−1M \le |\mathcal H| - 1M≤∣H∣−1. The sequence was arbitrary, so the supremum obeys the same bound. ■\blacksquare■

With four hypotheses, that is at most 3, which the adversary reached. For lesson 1’s ten one-feature hypotheses it is 9, and for a class of a million hypotheses it is 999,999. A bound that grows linearly with the size of the class is a poor promise. Can a learner do better by choosing more carefully which survivor to follow?

Halving: let the survivors vote

Here is a better idea. Instead of following one survivor, let all of them vote. If more survivors say junk than keep, predict junk; otherwise predict keep. Call it Halving, and when the vote is tied, let it predict junk.

Why the name? Think about what a mistake means for a voting learner. If Halving is wrong, the majority was wrong, and every hypothesis in the majority leaves the version space. At least half of the survivors are gone in one round. That is the whole idea, and it is worth seeing with numbers before any symbols.

Before reading the next table, try to play adversary yourself. Against Halving on H1\mathcal H_1H1​, what should the first message be? Sending 1000 again is a waste: three survivors say keep and one says junk, so Halving predicts keep, and calling it keep is no mistake, while calling it junk is a mistake that leaves only hFh_FhF​. The adversary wants a tie, so that whatever it says, it throws out only half.

111002 / 2102 (hU,hNh_U, h_NhU​,hN​)
200101 / 1101 (hNh_NhN​)
311111 / 0111
400011 / 0111
500000 / 1001
610011 / 0111

Two mistakes, and the count of survivors goes 4, 2, 1. Each mistake halved it.

H = "FLUN"
h = lambda name, x: int(x[H.index(name)])
halving = lambda V, x: int(2 * sum(h(n, x) for n in V)
                           >= len(V))
V, M = set(H), 0
s2 = [("1100", 0), ("0010", 0), ("1111", 1), ("0001", 1),
      ("0000", 0), ("1001", 1)]
for x, y in s2:
    p = halving(V, x)
    M += p != y
    V = {n for n in V if h(n, x) == y}
    print(x, p, y, len(V))
print(M)

It prints 1100 1 0 2, 0010 1 0 1, four rows with no mistake and one survivor, and then 2. The line 2 * sum(...) >= len(V) is the vote: junk when at least half of the survivors say junk, so a tie goes to junk.

That is the idea from above at work: every mistake at least halves the version space while the truth stays, and starting from ∣H∣|\mathcal H|∣H∣ you can halve only about log⁡2∣H∣\log_2 |\mathcal H|log2​∣H∣ times before you are down to one. The prediction rule, written out, is

pt=argmax⁡r∈{0,1}∣{h∈Vt:h(xt)=r}∣(ties go to 1).p_t = \operatorname*{argmax}_{r \in \{0, 1\}} \left| \{ h \in V_t : h(x_t) = r \} \right| \quad (\text{ties go to } 1).pt​=r∈{0,1}argmax​∣{h∈Vt​:h(xt​)=r}∣(ties go to 1).
  • rrr ranges over the two possible labels, 0 (keep) and 1 (junk).
  • {h∈Vt:h(xt)=r}\{ h \in V_t : h(x_t) = r \}{h∈Vt​:h(xt​)=r} is the set of survivors that say rrr on this message, and ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ counts them: the number of votes for rrr.
  • argmax⁡r\operatorname{argmax}_{r}argmaxr​ means “the value of rrr that makes the expression largest”: not the largest vote count itself, but the label that has it.

In plain words: predict the label that most survivors give this message. In row 1, V1V_1V1​ has four survivors; hFh_FhF​ and hLh_LhL​ say 1 on 1100 and hUh_UhU​, hNh_NhN​ say 0; the votes are 2 and 2, a tie, so p1=1p_1 = 1p1​=1.

Theorem (Halving’s mistake bound). For a finite class H\mathcal HH, MHalving(H)≤log⁡2∣H∣M_{\text{Halving}}(\mathcal H) \le \log_2 |\mathcal H|MHalving​(H)≤log2​∣H∣.

Proof. Take any realizable sequence and suppose Halving errs on round ttt. The hypotheses that said ptp_tpt​ on xtx_txt​ were wrong, so all of them leave; what remains, Vt+1V_{t+1}Vt+1​, is the set that said yt=1−pty_t = 1 - p_tyt​=1−pt​. Since ptp_tpt​ won the vote (or tied), the losing side had at most half the votes: ∣Vt+1∣≤∣Vt∣/2|V_{t+1}| \le |V_t|/2∣Vt+1​∣≤∣Vt​∣/2. On rounds without a mistake, ∣Vt+1∣≤∣Vt∣|V_{t+1}| \le |V_t|∣Vt+1​∣≤∣Vt​∣.

So if MMM mistakes happen in TTT rounds, the size has been halved at least MMM times, and the truth is still in it:

1≤∣VT+1∣≤∣H∣ 2−M.1 \le |V_{T+1}| \le |\mathcal H| \, 2^{-M}.1≤∣VT+1​∣≤∣H∣2−M.
  • ∣VT+1∣|V_{T+1}|∣VT+1​∣ is how many hypotheses survive all TTT rounds.
  • 2−M=1/2M2^{-M} = 1/2^M2−M=1/2M is what MMM halvings do to a count: multiply it by one half, MMM times.
  • The left inequality is the truth surviving; the right one is the halving.

In plain words: the survivors never run out, and every mistake at least halves them. In the table, ∣H1∣=4|\mathcal H_1| = 4∣H1​∣=4 and M=2M = 2M=2, so 4⋅2−2=14 \cdot 2^{-2} = 14⋅2−2=1, and indeed exactly one survivor is left: the inequality is tight. Multiplying both sides by 2M2^M2M gives 2M≤∣H∣2^M \le |\mathcal H|2M≤∣H∣, and taking log⁡2\log_2log2​ of both sides gives M≤log⁡2∣H∣M \le \log_2 |\mathcal H|M≤log2​∣H∣. ■\blacksquare■

For four hypotheses, log⁡24=2\log_2 4 = 2log2​4=2, which the adversary reached. For a million hypotheses it is about 19.9, so at most 19 mistakes, instead of Consistent’s 999,999. Exponentially better, by changing only which survivor we listen to.

You don’t have to trust either table to show the worst case. Python can play every possible adversary against each learner, trying every message and both labels in every round, and report the most mistakes any of them can force. That is MA(H1)M_A(\mathcal H_1)MA​(H1​) itself, the supremum, computed by brute force:

from functools import lru_cache
from itertools import product

X, H = list(product([0, 1], repeat=4)), "FLUN"
consistent = lambda V, x: x[H.index(min(V, key=H.index))]
halving = lambda V, x: int(2 * sum(x[H.index(h)] for h in V)
                           >= len(V))

@lru_cache(None)
def worst(V, learn):
    games = [(learn(V, x) != y) + worst(W, learn)
             for x in X for y in (0, 1)
             for W in [frozenset(h for h in V
                                 if x[H.index(h)] == y)]
             if W and W != V]
    return max(games, default=0)

print(worst(frozenset(H), consistent),
      worst(frozenset(H), halving))

It prints 3 2. The function worst is the adversary: from version space V, it tries each message x and each label y that keeps some hypothesis alive (if W), adds one if the learner got that round wrong, and recurses. Rounds where every survivor agrees teach nothing and cost nothing, so it skips them (W != V). The max is the sup⁡\supsup of the definition.

Notice something that separates the online world from the batch world. In lesson 2, any consistent hypothesis was a fine output. Online, choosing an arbitrary consistent hypothesis can cost exponentially more mistakes than choosing well.

The adversary’s plan is a tree

Halving’s bound depends on ∣H∣|\mathcal H|∣H∣, the number of hypotheses. Lesson 6 taught us to distrust counts: the class of thresholds is infinite, yet it is learnable from a few labels. Is there a better measure of how hard a class is online? To find it, look at the game from the adversary’s side.

The adversary wants to force a mistake on every one of the first few rounds. That part is easy: it waits for the prediction and announces the opposite label. The hard part is staying honest, so that at the end some hypothesis in H\mathcal HH agrees with every label it announced. Which message should it send on round 2? That depends on what happened on round 1, which depends on the learner. So the adversary’s plan is not a list of messages. It is a branching plan: “send v1v_1v1​ first; if the label turns out 0, send this next; if 1, send that.”

A branching plan is a binary tree. Each node holds a message. The adversary starts at the top node, the root, and sends its message. When the label is revealed, it moves to the left child if the label was 0 and to the right child if it was 1, and sends that node’s message next. The depth of the tree is the number of steps along a path from the root to the bottom. A tree in which every path has the same depth ddd and every node above the bottom has two children is complete, and it has 2d−12^d - 12d−1 nodes that hold messages: 1 for depth 1, 3 for depth 2.

Here is one for H1\mathcal H_1H1​, of depth 2. The root holds 1100, on which hFh_FhF​ and hLh_LhL​ say junk, hUh_UhU​ and hNh_NhN​ keep. Its left child, used after the label 0, holds 0010: the survivors are then hUh_UhU​ and hNh_NhN​, and 0010 splits them. Its right child, used after the label 1, holds 1000: the survivors are hFh_FhF​ and hLh_LhL​, and 1000 splits them. Every one of the four label paths (0 then 0, 0 then 1, 1 then 0, 1 then 1) is followed by exactly one hypothesis. So whatever the learner predicts, the adversary can announce the opposite label twice and still have a hypothesis that agrees. That is the depth-2 game from the Halving table, drawn as a plan.

[diagram:shattered-tree: built on the lesson page]

To write this down we need names for the nodes. Number them like a heap in a computer science course: the root is node 1, and node iii has left child 2i2i2i and right child 2i+12i + 12i+1. So the messages are v1,v2,…,v2d−1v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{2^d - 1}v1​,v2​,…,v2d−1​. If iti_tit​ is the node used on round ttt, then i1=1i_1 = 1i1​=1 and it+1=2it+yti_{t+1} = 2 i_t + y_tit+1​=2it​+yt​: double to go down a level, and add the label to go right on a 1. With labels y1=1y_1 = 1y1​=1, y2=0y_2 = 0y2​=0: i1=1i_1 = 1i1​=1, and i2=2⋅1+1=3i_2 = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 = 3i2​=2⋅1+1=3, the right child, holding 1000 in our tree.

from itertools import product

def path(ys):
    i = [1]
    for y in ys[:-1]:
        i.append(2 * i[-1] + y)
    return i

print(path((1, 0)))
v = {1: "1100", 2: "0010", 3: "1000"}
h = {n: (lambda x, k=k: int(x[k])) for k, n in enumerate("FLUN")}
print(all(any(all(h[n](v[i]) == y for i, y in zip(path(ys), ys))
              for n in h) for ys in product([0, 1], repeat=2)))

It prints [1, 3] (the path for labels 1 then 0) and True (our depth-2 tree for H1\mathcal H_1H1​ works: for each of the four label paths, some hypothesis agrees with all of it).

That last check is the property we need, and it gets a name.

Definition (shattered tree). A complete binary tree of depth ddd with messages v1,…,v2d−1v_1, \dots, v_{2^d - 1}v1​,…,v2d−1​ is shattered by H\mathcal HH if for every sequence of labels (y1,…,yd)∈{0,1}d(y_1, \dots, y_d) \in \{0, 1\}^d(y1​,…,yd​)∈{0,1}d there is some h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H with h(vit)=yth(v_{i_t}) = y_th(vit​​)=yt​ for every t∈[d]t \in [d]t∈[d], where iti_tit​ is the node the labels lead to.

In plain words: whichever way the labels go down the tree, some hypothesis in the class agrees with all of them. The word is borrowed from lesson 6, where a set of messages was shattered when the class could label it in every possible way; here it is a tree instead of a set, so later messages may depend on earlier labels.

Definition (Littlestone dimension). The Littlestone dimension of H\mathcal HH, written Ldim(H)\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)Ldim(H), is the largest depth ddd of a tree shattered by H\mathcal HH. If there are shattered trees of every depth, Ldim(H)=∞\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) = \inftyLdim(H)=∞.

The tree of depth 0 has no nodes, and the one label sequence of length 0 is matched by any hypothesis at all, so every nonempty class has Ldim≥0\mathrm{Ldim} \ge 0Ldim≥0. Our tree shows Ldim(H1)≥2\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H_1) \ge 2Ldim(H1​)≥2.

Try it before we prove anything. In the lab below, you play the adversary against Consistent, Halving, and a third learner we will meet shortly, on a class you choose, and you see how many mistakes you can force while keeping the labels honest. Watch your own moves: they will trace out a tree.

[lab: built on the lesson page]

No learner beats the tree

The first fact about the Littlestone dimension is the one the adversary’s story already told us.

Lemma (the tree lower bound). For every online learner AAA, MA(H)≥Ldim(H)M_A(\mathcal H) \ge \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)MA​(H)≥Ldim(H).

Proof. Let T=Ldim(H)T = \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)T=Ldim(H), assumed finite for now, and take a tree of depth TTT shattered by H\mathcal HH. The adversary walks it: on round ttt it sends xt=vitx_t = v_{i_t}xt​=vit​​, waits for ptp_tpt​, and announces yt=1−pty_t = 1 - p_tyt​=1−pt​. Every one of the TTT rounds is a mistake.

Is the sequence realizable? The labels (y1,…,yT)(y_1, \dots, y_T)(y1​,…,yT​) form one particular path, and the tree is shattered, so some h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H has h(vit)=yth(v_{i_t}) = y_th(vit​​)=yt​ for every ttt. That hhh is a legitimate truth. So this realizable sequence costs AAA exactly TTT mistakes, and the supremum MA(H)M_A(\mathcal H)MA​(H) is at least TTT. If Ldim(H)=∞\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) = \inftyLdim(H)=∞, run the same argument with a shattered tree of each depth TTT, so MA(H)≥TM_A(\mathcal H) \ge TMA​(H)≥T for every TTT, which means MA(H)=∞M_A(\mathcal H) = \inftyMA​(H)=∞. ■\blacksquare■

The learner can be as clever as it likes; it can even know the tree. It does not help, because the adversary moves after the learner has predicted.

Three classes, three dimensions

Let’s compute the dimension of a few classes, because the answers are surprising.

A finite class. A tree of depth ddd has 2d2^d2d label paths, and each path needs its own hypothesis (two different paths disagree on some node they both visit, so no hypothesis follows both). So a shattered tree of depth ddd needs ∣H∣≥2d|\mathcal H| \ge 2^d∣H∣≥2d, that is, Ldim(H)≤log⁡2∣H∣\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) \le \log_2 |\mathcal H|Ldim(H)≤log2​∣H∣. The tree lower bound and Halving’s bound give the same thing from the other side: Ldim(H)≤MHalving(H)≤log⁡2∣H∣\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) \le M_{\text{Halving}}(\mathcal H) \le \log_2 |\mathcal H|Ldim(H)≤MHalving​(H)≤log2​∣H∣.

One rogue sender. Suppose the junk this week comes from a single sender, and you don’t know which. Number the possible senders 1,…,d1, \dots, d1,…,d, let a message be just its sender, and let hjh_jhj​ say junk exactly when the sender is jjj. This is the class of singletons, with ddd hypotheses, so log⁡2d\log_2 dlog2​d can be large. Yet its Littlestone dimension is 1. A tree of depth 1 is just a root: send sender 1, and h1h_1h1​ says junk while h2h_2h2​ says keep, so depth 1 is shattered. For depth 2, the root holds some sender jjj; on the label 1 branch, only hjh_jhj​ is left, and one hypothesis cannot be split, so no depth-2 tree is shattered. The dimension can be far below log⁡2∣H∣\log_2 |\mathcal H|log2​∣H∣.

Thresholds on a score. Lesson 6 met thresholds on a spam score in [0,1][0, 1][0,1]: for each cut-off θ\thetaθ (“theta”), the hypothesis hθ(x)=1[x>θ]h_\theta(x) = \mathbb 1[x > \theta]hθ​(x)=1[x>θ] says junk when the score xxx is above θ\thetaθ. (The indicator 1[⋅]\mathbb 1[\cdot]1[⋅] is 1 when the statement inside is true and 0 when it is false, so h0.5(0.7)=1h_{0.5}(0.7) = 1h0.5​(0.7)=1, junk, and h0.5(0.2)=0h_{0.5}(0.2) = 0h0.5​(0.2)=0, keep.) Its VC dimension is 1, so in the batch world it is learnable from a handful of labels. Online, the adversary plays binary search. It sends score 1/21/21/2. Whatever the learner predicts, it announces the opposite. If it said junk, the threshold must be below 1/21/21/2, so it next sends 1/41/41/4; if keep, the threshold is at least 1/21/21/2, so it sends 3/43/43/4. And so on, halving the interval of thresholds that agree with everything so far. Every round is a mistake, and because the interval never becomes empty, some threshold agrees with all the labels, at every depth. So Ldim=∞\mathrm{Ldim} = \inftyLdim=∞, and no online learner has a mistake bound for thresholds.

from fractions import Fraction

def learner(x, lo, hi):
    return int(x > (2 * lo + hi) / 3)

lo, hi, stream, mistakes = Fraction(0), Fraction(1), [], 0
for t in range(20):
    x = (lo + hi) / 2
    p = learner(x, lo, hi)
    y = 1 - p
    mistakes += p != y
    stream.append((x, y))
    lo, hi = (lo, x) if y == 1 else (x, hi)
t_star = (lo + hi) / 2
print(mistakes, all(int(x > t_star) == y for x, y in stream))

It prints 20 True: twenty mistakes in twenty rounds, and the threshold θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆ in the middle of the final interval (t_star) agrees with every label. The learner here predicts with a threshold one third of the way into the current interval; swap in any rule you like. The exact fractions matter: with real numbers the binary search never runs out of room, and that is the density the proof uses.

Wow. A class that is easy for the batch filter is impossible for the online filter. The difference is that the batch filter got its examples at random, and an adversary is not random.

On a finite grid of scores the picture is in between. With 7 possible scores there are 8 thresholds and the dimension is 3; with 15 scores, 4. The next snippet computes Littlestone dimensions by brute force, using a recursion we prove in the next section; here it checks the three examples.

from functools import lru_cache
from itertools import product

@lru_cache(None)
def ldim(V):
    if not V:
        return -1
    n = len(next(iter(V)))
    splits = [[frozenset(h for h in V if h[x] == r)
               for r in (0, 1)] for x in range(n)]
    return max([1 + min(map(ldim, s)) for s in splits
                if all(s)], default=0)

X = list(product([0, 1], repeat=4))
one_feature = {tuple(x[j] for x in X) for j in range(4)}
singletons = {tuple(int(x == j) for x in range(8))
              for j in range(8)}
thresholds = lambda n: {tuple(int(x > t) for x in range(n))
                        for t in range(-1, n)}
print(ldim(frozenset(one_feature)), ldim(frozenset(singletons)),
      ldim(frozenset(thresholds(7))),
      ldim(frozenset(thresholds(15))))

It prints 2 1 3 4: H1\mathcal H_1H1​ has dimension 2 (so our tree was the deepest possible), eight singletons have dimension 1 while log⁡28=3\log_2 8 = 3log2​8=3, and thresholds on 7 and 15 grid points have dimensions 3 and 4, the depth of binary search. Each hypothesis is stored as the tuple of its labels on all messages.

The dimension splits at the root

To build the best learner, we need one structural fact. Pick a message xxx and split a class VVV by what its hypotheses say on xxx:

V(r)={h∈V:h(x)=r},r∈{0,1}.V^{(r)} = \{ h \in V : h(x) = r \}, \qquad r \in \{0, 1\}.V(r)={h∈V:h(x)=r},r∈{0,1}.
  • V(1)V^{(1)}V(1) is the part of VVV that says junk on xxx, and V(0)V^{(0)}V(0) the part that says keep. The superscript (r)(r)(r) names the label, not a power.

In plain words: split the class into the hypotheses that call xxx junk and those that call it keep. For H1\mathcal H_1H1​ and x=1100x = 1100x=1100: V(1)={hF,hL}V^{(1)} = \{h_F, h_L\}V(1)={hF​,hL​} and V(0)={hU,hN}V^{(0)} = \{h_U, h_N\}V(0)={hU​,hN​}.

Now look at a shattered tree with root xxx. Every label path starts with y1y_1y1​. The paths that start with 0 go into the left subtree, and they must be matched by hypotheses that also say 0 on xxx, that is, by V(0)V^{(0)}V(0). So the left subtree is a tree of depth d−1d - 1d−1 shattered by V(0)V^{(0)}V(0), and the right subtree is one shattered by V(1)V^{(1)}V(1). The converse holds too: put any message xxx at a root, hang a tree shattered by V(0)V^{(0)}V(0) on the left and one shattered by V(1)V^{(1)}V(1) on the right, both of depth d−1d - 1d−1, and the result is a tree of depth ddd shattered by VVV. (If the two subtrees have different depths, cut the deeper one down: the top part of a shattered tree is still shattered.)

Lemma (the root split). For any class VVV with Ldim(V)≥1\mathrm{Ldim}(V) \ge 1Ldim(V)≥1,

Ldim(V)=max⁡x  (1+min⁡{Ldim(V(0)),Ldim(V(1))}),\mathrm{Ldim}(V) = \max_{x} \; \Big( 1 + \min\big\{ \mathrm{Ldim}(V^{(0)}), \mathrm{Ldim}(V^{(1)}) \big\} \Big),Ldim(V)=xmax​(1+min{Ldim(V(0)),Ldim(V(1))}),

where the maximum runs over messages xxx on which both parts are nonempty, and V(0),V(1)V^{(0)}, V^{(1)}V(0),V(1) are the parts for that xxx.

  • min⁡{⋅,⋅}\min\{\cdot, \cdot\}min{⋅,⋅} takes the smaller of the two dimensions: a tree of depth ddd needs both subtrees to have depth d−1d - 1d−1, so the weaker side decides.
  • The 1+1 +1+ counts the root.
  • max⁡x\max_xmaxx​ lets the adversary choose the best root.

In plain words: the deepest tree puts at its root the message that splits the class into two parts that are both as rich as possible, and is one deeper than the poorer part. For H1\mathcal H_1H1​ and root 1100, both parts have two hypotheses and dimension 1, so the formula gives 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2. The ldim function above is this lemma, word for word: splits lists (V(0),V(1))(V^{(0)}, V^{(1)})(V(0),V(1)) for every message, if all(s) keeps those where both are nonempty, and 1 + min(map(ldim, s)) is the bracket. (It also returns 0 when no message splits the class and −1-1−1 for the empty class, a convention that makes the next section’s comparisons work.)

Proof. The paragraph before the lemma, in both directions: a shattered tree of depth d≥1d \ge 1d≥1 with root xxx makes the bracket for xxx at least ddd, and a bracket equal to ddd for some xxx builds a shattered tree of depth ddd under the root xxx. ■\blacksquare■

One more fact we will use: a subset can only lose dimension. If V′⊆VV' \subseteq VV′⊆V, every tree shattered by V′V'V′ is shattered by VVV, so Ldim(V′)≤Ldim(V)\mathrm{Ldim}(V') \le \mathrm{Ldim}(V)Ldim(V′)≤Ldim(V).

The Standard Optimal Algorithm

Halving splits the version space into the part that says junk and the part that says keep, and predicts with the bigger part. Bigger meant more hypotheses. What if “bigger” meant “higher Littlestone dimension” instead? That is the whole change, and the learner it gives is called the Standard Optimal Algorithm, SOA for short.

SOA(H):
  V_1 ← H
  for t = 1, 2, ...:
    receive x_t
    for r in {0, 1}: V_t^(r) ← {h in V_t : h(x_t) = r}
    predict p_t ← argmax over r of Ldim(V_t^(r))   (ties: 1)
    receive y_t
    V_{t+1} ← V_t^(y_t)

Why should this help? Halving fights the number of survivors. But the number is not what the adversary needs; it needs a deep shattered tree. SOA fights the dimension directly: it always predicts with the side that would leave the adversary the richer game, so that if it is wrong, the adversary is left with the poorer one.

Lemma (SOA’s mistake bound). MSOA(H)≤Ldim(H)M_{\text{SOA}}(\mathcal H) \le \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)MSOA​(H)≤Ldim(H).

Proof. It is enough to show that every mistake lowers the dimension of the version space by at least one: Ldim(Vt+1)≤Ldim(Vt)−1\mathrm{Ldim}(V_{t+1}) \le \mathrm{Ldim}(V_t) - 1Ldim(Vt+1​)≤Ldim(Vt​)−1 whenever pt≠ytp_t \neq y_tpt​=yt​. Since h⋆h^\starh⋆ is always in the version space, the dimension never drops below 0, so it can drop at most Ldim(H)\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)Ldim(H) times.

Suppose round ttt is a mistake, and suppose for contradiction that the dimension did not drop. Write d=Ldim(Vt)d = \mathrm{Ldim}(V_t)d=Ldim(Vt​). Since Vt+1=Vt(yt)⊆VtV_{t+1} = V_t^{(y_t)} \subseteq V_tVt+1​=Vt(yt​)​⊆Vt​, its dimension is at most ddd; not dropping means Ldim(Vt(yt))=d\mathrm{Ldim}(V_t^{(y_t)}) = dLdim(Vt(yt​)​)=d. SOA predicted ptp_tpt​ because its side had the larger (or tied) dimension, so Ldim(Vt(pt))≥Ldim(Vt(yt))=d\mathrm{Ldim}(V_t^{(p_t)}) \ge \mathrm{Ldim}(V_t^{(y_t)}) = dLdim(Vt(pt​)​)≥Ldim(Vt(yt​)​)=d, and it is also at most ddd as a subset. So both parts have dimension exactly ddd, and ptp_tpt​ and yty_tyt​ are the two different labels, so these are Vt(0)V_t^{(0)}Vt(0)​ and Vt(1)V_t^{(1)}Vt(1)​.

Now use the root split with root xtx_txt​: both parts are nonempty (they have dimension d≥0d \ge 0d≥0), so Ldim(Vt)≥1+min⁡{d,d}=d+1\mathrm{Ldim}(V_t) \ge 1 + \min\{d, d\} = d + 1Ldim(Vt​)≥1+min{d,d}=d+1. That contradicts Ldim(Vt)=d\mathrm{Ldim}(V_t) = dLdim(Vt​)=d. ■\blacksquare■

Put the two lemmas side by side. Every learner can be forced into Ldim(H)\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)Ldim(H) mistakes, and SOA never makes more.

Theorem (the Littlestone dimension characterizes online learnability). For every class H\mathcal HH, MSOA(H)=Ldim(H)M_{\text{SOA}}(\mathcal H) = \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)MSOA​(H)=Ldim(H), and no online learner AAA has MA(H)<Ldim(H)M_A(\mathcal H) < \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)MA​(H)<Ldim(H). In particular, H\mathcal HH is online learnable exactly when Ldim(H)<∞\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) < \inftyLdim(H)<∞.

Does SOA ever beat Halving in practice? Here is a class built to show it. Take eight messages, x0,u,v,s1,…,s5x_0, u, v, s_1, \dots, s_5x0​,u,v,s1​,…,s5​. Part A of the class is five hypotheses, “junk exactly when the message is sjs_jsj​”, one per jjj: singletons, dimension 1. Part B is four hypotheses that say junk on x0x_0x0​, keep on every sjs_jsj​, and every one of the four possible label pairs on uuu and vvv: dimension 2. When x0x_0x0​ arrives, part A (five hypotheses) says keep and part B (four) says junk. Halving counts heads and predicts keep; the adversary says junk, and is left with part B and two more forced mistakes. SOA sees that part B has the higher dimension and predicts junk; if the adversary says keep, it is left with the singletons and can force only one more mistake.

from functools import lru_cache

A = [(0, 0, 0) + tuple(int(i == j) for i in range(5))
     for j in range(5)]
B = [(1, u, v) + (0,) * 5 for u in (0, 1) for v in (0, 1)]
part = lambda V, x, r: frozenset(h for h in V if h[x] == r)
moves = lambda V: [(x, y, W) for x in range(8) for y in (0, 1)
                   for W in [part(V, x, y)] if W and W != V]

@lru_cache(None)
def ldim(V):
    return max([1 + min(ldim(W), ldim(V - W))
                for x, y, W in moves(V)], default=0)

@lru_cache(None)
def worst(V, learn):
    return max([(learn(V, x) != y) + worst(W, learn)
                for x, y, W in moves(V)], default=0)

big = lambda f, V, x: int(f(part(V, x, 1)) >= f(part(V, x, 0)))
halving = lambda V, x: big(len, V, x)
soa = lambda V, x: big(ldim, V, x)
H = frozenset(A + B)
print(len(H), ldim(H), worst(H, halving), worst(H, soa))

It prints 9 2 3 2: nine hypotheses, dimension 2, the best adversary forces 3 mistakes on Halving and only 2 on SOA. The only difference between the two learners is the function big compares the parts with: len for Halving, ldim for SOA.

A word on cost, since we promised to ignore it and should be honest about what we ignored. SOA needs the Littlestone dimension of two sets on every round, and computing it by the root split recursion visits a game tree that can be exponentially large. SOA is the optimal learner in mistakes, not in time.

Littlestone dimension against VC dimension

Thresholds showed that online learning can be much harder than batch learning. Is it ever easier? No, and the proof is a picture.

Theorem. For every class H\mathcal HH, VCdim(H)≤Ldim(H)\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal H) \le \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)VCdim(H)≤Ldim(H), and the gap can be arbitrarily large.

Proof. Recall from lesson 6 that a set {x1,…,xd}\{x_1, \dots, x_d\}{x1​,…,xd​} is shattered by H\mathcal HH when every one of the 2d2^d2d labellings of it is given by some hypothesis, and VCdim(H)\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal H)VCdim(H) is the largest such ddd. Take a shattered set of size ddd and build a complete tree of depth ddd whose nodes on level iii all hold xix_ixi​. Whatever the label path (y1,…,yd)(y_1, \dots, y_d)(y1​,…,yd​), the messages visited are x1,…,xdx_1, \dots, x_dx1​,…,xd​ in order, and the set is shattered, so some hhh gives h(xi)=yih(x_i) = y_ih(xi​)=yi​ for all iii. The tree is shattered, so Ldim(H)≥d\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) \ge dLdim(H)≥d. For the gap: thresholds on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] have VC dimension 1 and Littlestone dimension ∞\infty∞. ■\blacksquare■

For H1\mathcal H_1H1​: the set {1100,1010}\{1100, 1010\}{1100,1010} is shattered, since hF,hL,hU,hNh_F, h_L, h_U, h_NhF​,hL​,hU​,hN​ give it the labels (1, 1), (1, 0), (0, 1), (0, 0). The tree with 1100 at the root and 1010 at both children is then shattered.

from itertools import product

h = {n: (lambda x, k=k: int(x[k])) for k, n in enumerate("FLUN")}
x1, x2 = "1100", "1010"
print(sorted((h[n](x1), h[n](x2)) for n in h))
tree = {1: x1, 2: x2, 3: x2}
path = lambda ys: [1, 2 + ys[0]]
print(all(any(all(h[n](tree[i]) == y
                  for i, y in zip(path(ys), ys)) for n in h)
          for ys in product([0, 1], repeat=2)))

It prints [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)] (all four labellings of the set appear) and True (the tree built from the set is shattered). The VC dimension asks for a tree whose messages may not depend on the labels; the Littlestone dimension lets them depend on the labels, which is exactly the extra power an adversary has.

When no hypothesis is perfect

Realizability was a comfortable assumption, and the spammers are not comfortable people. Real mail is noisy: some users report newsletters they subscribed to, a few junk messages look exactly like real ones, and no hypothesis in any class you can afford agrees with every label. Lesson 3 met the same problem in the batch world and answered it with agnostic learning: stop asking for a perfect hypothesis and ask instead to do almost as well as the best one in the class.

The online version of “almost as well as the best one” is called regret. The idea first, with numbers. Suppose that after 1,000 rounds your filter has made 130 mistakes. Looking back, you check every hypothesis in H\mathcal HH and find that the best of them, had you followed it from the first round, would have made 100. You are “sorry” about 30 mistakes. That 30 is your regret with respect to that hypothesis. If the worst-case regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds, say like T\sqrt TT​, then the regret per round goes to zero, and in the long run the filter is as good as the best hypothesis in hindsight, against any sequence at all.

In symbols, for an online learner AAA, a hypothesis hhh and a number of rounds TTT,

RegretA(h,T)=sup⁡(x1,y1),…,(xT,yT)[∑t=1T∣pt−yt∣−∑t=1T∣h(xt)−yt∣],RegretA(H,T)=sup⁡h∈HRegretA(h,T).\mathrm{Regret}_A(h, T) = \sup_{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_T, y_T)} \left[ \sum_{t=1}^T |p_t - y_t| - \sum_{t=1}^T |h(x_t) - y_t| \right], \qquad \mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathcal H, T) = \sup_{h \in \mathcal H} \mathrm{Regret}_A(h, T).RegretA​(h,T)=(x1​,y1​),…,(xT​,yT​)sup​[t=1∑T​∣pt​−yt​∣−t=1∑T​∣h(xt​)−yt​∣],RegretA​(H,T)=h∈Hsup​RegretA​(h,T).

Read it from the inside out.

  • ∣pt−yt∣|p_t - y_t|∣pt​−yt​∣ is the learner’s loss on round ttt. With predictions and labels in {0,1}\{0, 1\}{0,1}, it is 1 for a mistake and 0 otherwise.
  • ∑t=1T\sum_{t=1}^T∑t=1T​ adds that loss over the rounds 1,…,T1, \dots, T1,…,T: the first sum is the learner’s mistake count, and the second, with h(xt)h(x_t)h(xt​) in place of ptp_tpt​, is the mistake count of the fixed hypothesis hhh on the same messages.
  • The bracket is the difference: how many more mistakes the learner made than hhh.
  • sup⁡\supsup over the sequence (x1,y1),…,(xT,yT)(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_T, y_T)(x1​,y1​),…,(xT​,yT​) takes the worst sequence of TTT rounds for the learner. No realizability this time: any labels at all.
  • sup⁡h∈H\sup_{h \in \mathcal H}suph∈H​ then takes the hypothesis that makes the learner look worst, which is the best hypothesis in hindsight.

In plain words: the regret is how many more mistakes the learner makes than the best hypothesis in the class, on the worst sequence of TTT rounds. With the numbers above, 130−100=30130 - 100 = 30130−100=30 on that sequence; the regret is the largest such difference any sequence can produce. The goal is a regret that grows sublinearly in TTT, meaning RegretA(H,T)/T→0\mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathcal H, T)/T \to 0RegretA​(H,T)/T→0 as T→∞T \to \inftyT→∞.

The flipping adversary wins again

Is sublinear regret possible? Not for any learner that decides deterministically, even for a class of two hypotheses. Take the smallest interesting class: h0h_0h0​ says keep on every message and h1h_1h1​ says junk on every message. The adversary plays the opening trick again: it waits for the prediction and announces the opposite label. The learner makes TTT mistakes in TTT rounds.

And the best hypothesis in hindsight? Out of the TTT labels, either at least half are 0 or at least half are 1. Whichever label is in the majority, the constant hypothesis that always says it is wrong on at most T/2T/2T/2 rounds. So the regret is at least T−T/2=T/2T - T/2 = T/2T−T/2=T/2, which is linear in TTT. This is Cover’s impossibility result.

[diagram:cover: built on the lesson page]

def follow_the_majority(labels):
    return int(2 * sum(labels) > len(labels))

T, labels, mistakes = 1000, [], 0
for t in range(T):
    p = follow_the_majority(labels)
    y = 1 - p
    mistakes += p != y
    labels.append(y)
best = min(sum(labels), T - sum(labels))
print(mistakes, best, mistakes - best)
coin = sum(abs(0.5 - y) for y in labels)
print(coin, coin - best)

It prints 1000 500 500: a learner that predicts the majority label so far makes 1,000 mistakes, the better constant hypothesis makes 500, and the regret is 500, half of TTT. The second line is a hint of the way out. A learner that ignores everything and predicts junk with probability one half would expect to lose half a mistake per round, 500 here, the same as the best constant. Randomness is something the flipping adversary cannot read in advance. (The plain coin is not the answer, though: if every label were junk, the coin would still lose 500 while h1h_1h1​ lost nothing.)

The same thing happens with more hypotheses. Here is a deterministic learner with ten experts to choose from (we define experts properly below; for now think of ten hypotheses) that follows whichever one has the fewest mistakes so far. The adversary makes the one it picked wrong, every round:

d, T = 10, 2000
totals, paid = [0] * d, 0
for t in range(T):
    pick = min(range(d), key=lambda i: totals[i])
    v = [int(i == pick) for i in range(d)]
    paid += v[pick]
    totals = [s + vi for s, vi in zip(totals, v)]
print(paid, min(totals), paid - min(totals))

It prints 2000 200 1800: the learner pays on every one of the 2,000 rounds, the punishment is spread over all ten experts so the best of them pays only 200, and the regret is 1,800, which is 0.9 T0.9\,T0.9T. Following the leader is the most natural deterministic strategy there is, and it is the one the adversary eats first.

Let the learner flip a coin

So we give the learner a coin, and we change one rule of the game: the adversary must choose the label yty_tyt​ without seeing the outcome of the learner’s coin on round ttt. It may know the learner’s code, its probabilities, and every coin flip of earlier rounds. It just cannot see this round’s flip before it commits. For a spam filter that is realistic: the spammer sends the message before the filter decides.

Now the learner announces a number pt∈[0,1]p_t \in [0, 1]pt​∈[0,1], the probability with which it will say junk, and then draws its actual label y^t\hat y_ty^​t​, which is 1 with probability ptp_tpt​. How often is it wrong? If the true label is 1, it is wrong when it draws 0, with probability 1−pt1 - p_t1−pt​. If the true label is 0, it is wrong when it draws 1, with probability ptp_tpt​. Both cases are the same formula:

P[y^t≠yt]=∣pt−yt∣.\mathbb P[\hat y_t \neq y_t] = |p_t - y_t|.P[y^​t​=yt​]=∣pt​−yt​∣.
  • y^t\hat y_ty^​t​ (“y hat”) is the label the learner actually outputs after flipping its coin; ptp_tpt​ is now the coin’s bias, not a label.
  • P[⋅]\mathbb P[\cdot]P[⋅] is the probability of the event in brackets, over the learner’s own coin only. The message and label are fixed when the coin is flipped.

In plain words: a learner that says junk with probability ptp_tpt​ is wrong with probability equal to the distance between ptp_tpt​ and the true label. With pt=0.3p_t = 0.3pt​=0.3: if the message is junk, it misses with probability 0.70.70.7; if it is keep, it raises a false alarm with probability 0.30.30.3.

import random

rng, p, n = random.Random(4), 0.3, 100_000
for y in (1, 0):
    wrong = sum((rng.random() < p) != y for _ in range(n))
    print(y, round(wrong / n, 3), abs(p - y))

It prints 1 0.699 0.7 and 0 0.301 0.3: the measured error rates over 100,000 coin flips land on ∣p−y∣|p - y|∣p−y∣. So the regret formula above does not change at all. We simply let ptp_tpt​ be any number in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] and read ∑t∣pt−yt∣\sum_t |p_t - y_t|∑t​∣pt​−yt​∣ as the learner’s expected number of mistakes, the expectation being over its own coins.

Weighted-Majority

The learner that takes advantage of the coin is called Weighted-Majority, and it is easiest to describe in a slightly more general setting called prediction with expert advice. There are ddd experts: advisers whose advice the learner may follow. On each round, the learner chooses a probability distribution over the experts, a vector of weights w(t)=(w1(t),…,wd(t))\mathbf w^{(t)} = (w_1^{(t)}, \dots, w_d^{(t)})w(t)=(w1(t)​,…,wd(t)​) with every wi(t)≥0w_i^{(t)} \ge 0wi(t)​≥0 and ∑iwi(t)=1\sum_i w_i^{(t)} = 1∑i​wi(t)​=1, and follows expert iii with probability wi(t)w_i^{(t)}wi(t)​. Then the adversary reveals a cost for every expert, a vector vt∈[0,1]d\mathbf v_t \in [0, 1]^dvt​∈[0,1]d, where vt,iv_{t,i}vt,i​ is what following expert iii would have cost this round. The learner’s expected cost is the weighted average of the experts’ costs, ∑iwi(t)vt,i=⟨w(t),vt⟩\sum_i w_i^{(t)} v_{t,i} = \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle∑i​wi(t)​vt,i​=⟨w(t),vt​⟩, using the inner product of lesson 9.

For the filter, the experts will be hypotheses and the cost of an expert will be 1 if it got the message wrong and 0 if it got it right. But the general version is cleaner to analyse, so let’s stay with it.

The idea of Weighted-Majority, in words: trust every expert equally at first, and every time an expert costs something, shrink its trust by a factor that depends on how much it cost. Experts that keep being wrong fade away exponentially fast, while experts that are mostly right keep their weight. Because the learner always spreads its bets, the adversary cannot single out one choice to punish.

Weighted-Majority(d, T):
  η ← sqrt(2 log(d) / T)
  w̃^(1) ← (1, ..., 1)
  for t = 1, 2, ..., T:
    Z_t ← sum of w̃^(t)_i over i
    w^(t) ← w̃^(t) / Z_t
    choose expert i with probability w^(t)_i
    receive costs v_t in [0, 1]^d
    pay ⟨w^(t), v_t⟩
    for every i: w̃^(t+1)_i ← w̃^(t)_i · exp(−η v_{t,i})

The update is the heart of it:

w~i(t+1)=w~i(t)e−ηvt,i,w(t)=w~(t)Zt,Zt=∑i=1dw~i(t).\tilde w_i^{(t+1)} = \tilde w_i^{(t)} e^{-\eta v_{t,i}}, \qquad \mathbf w^{(t)} = \frac{\tilde{\mathbf w}^{(t)}}{Z_t}, \quad Z_t = \sum_{i=1}^d \tilde w_i^{(t)}.w~i(t+1)​=w~i(t)​e−ηvt,i​,w(t)=Zt​w~(t)​,Zt​=i=1∑d​w~i(t)​.
  • w~i(t)\tilde w_i^{(t)}w~i(t)​ (“w tilde”) is expert iii’s raw trust before round ttt; it starts at 1.
  • e−ηvt,ie^{-\eta v_{t,i}}e−ηvt,i​ is the shrink factor: 1 when the cost is 0, and e−η≈1−ηe^{-\eta} \approx 1 - \etae−η≈1−η when the cost is 1. The number η>0\eta > 0η>0 is the step size, as in lessons 14 and 15, and it sets how hard one bad round is punished. The pseudocode sets it to 2log⁡(d)/T\sqrt{2 \log(d)/T}2log(d)/T​, with log⁡\loglog the natural logarithm, as everywhere in this course.
  • ZtZ_tZt​ is the total raw trust, and dividing by it turns the raw trusts into weights that add up to 1: w(t)\mathbf w^{(t)}w(t) is a probability distribution.

In plain words: multiply each expert’s trust by e−ηe^{-\eta}e−η raised to its cost, then rescale so the trusts add up to one. With two experts, η=0.5\eta = 0.5η=0.5, and a first round where expert 1 costs 1 and expert 2 costs 0: the raw trusts become e−0.5≈0.607e^{-0.5} \approx 0.607e−0.5≈0.607 and 1, so the weights become 0.607/1.607≈0.380.607/1.607 \approx 0.380.607/1.607≈0.38 and 1/1.607≈0.621/1.607 \approx 0.621/1.607≈0.62.

Let’s watch it against a hostile adversary. Ten experts, 2,000 rounds. On every round, the adversary looks at the weights and charges cost 1 to the five experts the learner currently trusts most, and cost 0 to the other five. A deterministic learner would be destroyed by this, as we saw. Weighted-Majority:

from math import exp, log, sqrt

d, T = 10, 2000
eta = sqrt(2 * log(d) / T)
w_tilde, paid, totals = [1.0] * d, 0.0, [0.0] * d
for t in range(T):
    Z = sum(w_tilde)
    w = [wi / Z for wi in w_tilde]
    trusted = sorted(range(d), key=lambda i: -w[i])[:d // 2]
    v = [1.0 if i in trusted else 0.0 for i in range(d)]
    paid += sum(wi * vi for wi, vi in zip(w, v))
    totals = [s + vi for s, vi in zip(totals, v)]
    w_tilde = [wi * exp(-eta * vi) for wi, vi in zip(w_tilde, v)]
bound = sqrt(2 * log(d) * T)
print(round(paid, 1), min(totals), round(paid - min(totals), 1),
      round(bound, 1))

It prints 1012.0 1000.0 12.0 96.0. The learner’s expected cost is 1,012, the best expert in hindsight paid 1,000, so the regret is 12, well under the 96 that the theorem below promises. Each line of the loop is a line of the pseudocode: Z is ZtZ_tZt​, w is w(t)\mathbf w^{(t)}w(t), paid accumulates ⟨w(t),vt⟩\langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle⟨w(t),vt​⟩, and the last line is the update.

[diagram:weights: built on the lesson page]

Theorem (Weighted-Majority’s regret). If T>2log⁡dT > 2 \log dT>2logd, Weighted-Majority with η=2log⁡(d)/T\eta = \sqrt{2 \log(d)/T}η=2log(d)/T​ satisfies, for every sequence of cost vectors,

∑t=1T⟨w(t),vt⟩−min⁡i∈[d]∑t=1Tvt,i≤2log⁡(d) T.\sum_{t=1}^T \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle - \min_{i \in [d]} \sum_{t=1}^T v_{t,i} \le \sqrt{2 \log(d) \, T}.t=1∑T​⟨w(t),vt​⟩−i∈[d]min​t=1∑T​vt,i​≤2log(d)T​.
  • The first sum is the learner’s total expected cost over TTT rounds.
  • ∑tvt,i\sum_t v_{t,i}∑t​vt,i​ is expert iii’s total cost, and min⁡i∈[d]\min_{i \in [d]}mini∈[d]​ picks the cheapest expert in hindsight.

In plain words: over any TTT rounds, Weighted-Majority pays at most 2log⁡(d) T\sqrt{2 \log(d)\, T}2log(d)T​ more than the best expert, whatever the adversary does. With ten experts and 2,000 rounds, 2⋅2.303⋅2000≈96\sqrt{2 \cdot 2.303 \cdot 2000} \approx 962⋅2.303⋅2000​≈96, so at most about 4.8% of the rounds, and that fraction keeps shrinking like 1/T1/\sqrt T1/T​.

Proof. The plan: watch the total raw trust ZtZ_tZt​. We show it must fall quickly whenever the learner pays a lot (an upper bound), and it cannot fall below the trust of the best expert (a lower bound). Squeezed between the two, the learner’s cost cannot run far ahead of the best expert’s.

Step 1: one round of shrinking. Divide the new total by the old one:

log⁡Zt+1Zt=log⁡∑iw~i(t)Zte−ηvt,i=log⁡∑iwi(t)e−ηvt,i.\log \frac{Z_{t+1}}{Z_t} = \log \sum_i \frac{\tilde w_i^{(t)}}{Z_t} e^{-\eta v_{t,i}} = \log \sum_i w_i^{(t)} e^{-\eta v_{t,i}}.logZt​Zt+1​​=logi∑​Zt​w~i(t)​​e−ηvt,i​=logi∑​wi(t)​e−ηvt,i​.

The first equality writes Zt+1=∑iw~i(t)e−ηvt,iZ_{t+1} = \sum_i \tilde w_i^{(t)} e^{-\eta v_{t,i}}Zt+1​=∑i​w~i(t)​e−ηvt,i​, which is the update, and divides each term by ZtZ_tZt​. The second recognizes w~i(t)/Zt\tilde w_i^{(t)}/Z_tw~i(t)​/Zt​ as the weight wi(t)w_i^{(t)}wi(t)​. In words: the log of how much the total trust shrank this round is the log of the weighted average of the shrink factors. In the snippet above, on round 1 every weight is 0.1 and five experts shrink by e−0.048≈0.953e^{-0.048} \approx 0.953e−0.048≈0.953, so the average shrink factor is 0.5+0.5⋅0.953=0.9770.5 + 0.5 \cdot 0.953 = 0.9770.5+0.5⋅0.953=0.977.

Step 2: a quadratic bound on the exponential. For 0≤a≤10 \le a \le 10≤a≤1, e−a≤1−a+a2/2e^{-a} \le 1 - a + a^2/2e−a≤1−a+a2/2. Why: the difference g(a)=1−a+a2/2−e−ag(a) = 1 - a + a^2/2 - e^{-a}g(a)=1−a+a2/2−e−a has g(0)=0g(0) = 0g(0)=0 and slope g′(a)=−1+a+e−ag'(a) = -1 + a + e^{-a}g′(a)=−1+a+e−a, which is at least 0 because e−a≥1−ae^{-a} \ge 1 - ae−a≥1−a (the exponential lies above its tangent line at 0, the convexity of lesson 12). So ggg never decreases from 0. Apply it with a=ηvt,ia = \eta v_{t,i}a=ηvt,i​, which is in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] because vt,i∈[0,1]v_{t,i} \in [0, 1]vt,i​∈[0,1] and η<1\eta < 1η<1 (that is what T>2log⁡dT > 2 \log dT>2logd buys: η2=2log⁡(d)/T<1\eta^2 = 2 \log(d)/T < 1η2=2log(d)/T<1). Since the weights add up to 1,

log⁡Zt+1Zt≤log⁡∑iwi(t)(1−ηvt,i+η2vt,i22)=log⁡(1−b),b=∑iwi(t)(ηvt,i−η2vt,i22).\log \frac{Z_{t+1}}{Z_t} \le \log \sum_i w_i^{(t)} \left( 1 - \eta v_{t,i} + \frac{\eta^2 v_{t,i}^2}{2} \right) = \log(1 - b), \qquad b = \sum_i w_i^{(t)} \left( \eta v_{t,i} - \frac{\eta^2 v_{t,i}^2}{2} \right).logZt​Zt+1​​≤logi∑​wi(t)​(1−ηvt,i​+2η2vt,i2​​)=log(1−b),b=i∑​wi(t)​(ηvt,i​−2η2vt,i2​​).

Here log⁡\loglog is increasing, so a bigger inside gives a bigger log; and ∑iwi(t)⋅1=1\sum_i w_i^{(t)} \cdot 1 = 1∑i​wi(t)​⋅1=1 pulled the 1 out front. The new name bbb is just the weighted average of ηv−η2v2/2\eta v - \eta^2 v^2/2ηv−η2v2/2. In words: the shrink per round is at most log⁡(1−b)\log(1 - b)log(1−b), where bbb is roughly η\etaη times the learner’s cost.

Step 3: log⁡(1−b)≤−b\log(1 - b) \le -blog(1−b)≤−b. This holds for every b<1b < 1b<1, because 1−b≤e−b1 - b \le e^{-b}1−b≤e−b (the same tangent-line fact) and log⁡\loglog is increasing. Our bbb is less than 1 since each term ηv−η2v2/2≤η<1\eta v - \eta^2 v^2/2 \le \eta < 1ηv−η2v2/2≤η<1. So

log⁡Zt+1Zt≤−η⟨w(t),vt⟩+η22∑iwi(t)vt,i2≤−η⟨w(t),vt⟩+η22.\log \frac{Z_{t+1}}{Z_t} \le -\eta \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle + \frac{\eta^2}{2} \sum_i w_i^{(t)} v_{t,i}^2 \le -\eta \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle + \frac{\eta^2}{2}.logZt​Zt+1​​≤−η⟨w(t),vt​⟩+2η2​i∑​wi(t)​vt,i2​≤−η⟨w(t),vt​⟩+2η2​.

The first inequality expands −b-b−b into its two parts, the first being η\etaη times the learner’s expected cost. The second uses vt,i2≤1v_{t,i}^2 \le 1vt,i2​≤1 and weights that add up to 1. In words: every round, the total trust shrinks (in log terms) by at least η\etaη times what the learner paid, minus a small η2/2\eta^2/2η2/2. On round 1 of the hostile run (η≈0.048\eta \approx 0.048η≈0.048, the learner pays 0.5), the true shrink and the three bounds of Steps 2 and 3 read −0.023705≤−0.023696≤−0.023417≤−0.022841-0.023705 \le -0.023696 \le -0.023417 \le -0.022841−0.023705≤−0.023696≤−0.023417≤−0.022841.

from math import exp, log

grid = [k / 1000 for k in range(1001)]
print(all(exp(-a) <= 1 - a + a * a / 2 for a in grid))
print(all(log(1 - b) <= -b for b in grid[:-1] + [-0.5, -3]))
print(round(1 - 1 + 1 / 2 - exp(-1), 3))

It prints True, True and 0.132: both inequalities hold on a fine grid (including some negative bbb), and at a=1a = 1a=1 the quadratic is 0.132 above e−1e^{-1}e−1, so the bound is not tight but is never wrong.

Step 4: add up the rounds. Summing Step 3 over t=1,…,Tt = 1, \dots, Tt=1,…,T, the left side telescopes: log⁡(Z2/Z1)+log⁡(Z3/Z2)+⋯=log⁡ZT+1−log⁡Z1\log(Z_2/Z_1) + \log(Z_3/Z_2) + \dots = \log Z_{T+1} - \log Z_1log(Z2​/Z1​)+log(Z3​/Z2​)+⋯=logZT+1​−logZ1​. And Z1=dZ_1 = dZ1​=d, since every raw trust starts at 1. So

log⁡ZT+1−log⁡d≤−η∑t=1T⟨w(t),vt⟩+Tη22.\log Z_{T+1} - \log d \le -\eta \sum_{t=1}^T \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle + \frac{T \eta^2}{2}.logZT+1​−logd≤−ηt=1∑T​⟨w(t),vt​⟩+2Tη2​.

In words: the total trust has fallen by at least η\etaη times the learner’s total cost, minus Tη2/2T\eta^2/2Tη2/2.

Step 5: the best expert holds the total up. Unrolling the update, expert iii’s raw trust after TTT rounds is w~i(T+1)=e−η∑tvt,i\tilde w_i^{(T+1)} = e^{-\eta \sum_t v_{t,i}}w~i(T+1)​=e−η∑t​vt,i​. The total is at least its largest term, so

log⁡ZT+1=log⁡∑ie−η∑tvt,i≥log⁡max⁡ie−η∑tvt,i=−ηmin⁡i∑tvt,i.\log Z_{T+1} = \log \sum_i e^{-\eta \sum_t v_{t,i}} \ge \log \max_i e^{-\eta \sum_t v_{t,i}} = -\eta \min_i \sum_t v_{t,i}.logZT+1​=logi∑​e−η∑t​vt,i​≥logimax​e−η∑t​vt,i​=−ηimin​t∑​vt,i​.

The last step: the largest e−ηce^{-\eta c}e−ηc belongs to the smallest cost ccc, and log⁡e−ηc=−ηc\log e^{-\eta c} = -\eta cloge−ηc=−ηc. In words: the total trust is at least the trust of the best expert, which has only shrunk by its own cost.

Step 6: squeeze. Steps 4 and 5 bound log⁡ZT+1\log Z_{T+1}logZT+1​ from both sides:

−ηmin⁡i∑tvt,i−log⁡d≤−η∑t⟨w(t),vt⟩+Tη22.-\eta \min_i \sum_t v_{t,i} - \log d \le -\eta \sum_t \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle + \frac{T \eta^2}{2}.−ηimin​t∑​vt,i​−logd≤−ηt∑​⟨w(t),vt​⟩+2Tη2​.

Move the learner’s cost to the left and divide by η>0\eta > 0η>0:

∑t⟨w(t),vt⟩−min⁡i∑tvt,i≤log⁡dη+ηT2.\sum_t \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle - \min_i \sum_t v_{t,i} \le \frac{\log d}{\eta} + \frac{\eta T}{2}.t∑​⟨w(t),vt​⟩−imin​t∑​vt,i​≤ηlogd​+2ηT​.

This holds for every η∈(0,1)\eta \in (0, 1)η∈(0,1), and it is the form we will use in the lab. Read it as two forces: a small η\etaη learns slowly (the first term, the cost of starting with no idea which expert is good), and a large η\etaη overreacts (the second term). With η=2log⁡(d)/T\eta = \sqrt{2 \log(d)/T}η=2log(d)/T​, the first term is log⁡d⋅T/(2log⁡d)=Tlog⁡(d)/2\log d \cdot \sqrt{T/(2 \log d)} = \sqrt{T \log(d)/2}logd⋅T/(2logd)​=Tlog(d)/2​ and the second is T22log⁡(d)/T=Tlog⁡(d)/2\frac T2 \sqrt{2 \log(d)/T} = \sqrt{T \log(d)/2}2T​2log(d)/T​=Tlog(d)/2​, and together they make 2Tlog⁡(d)/2=2log⁡(d) T2\sqrt{T \log(d)/2} = \sqrt{2 \log(d)\, T}2Tlog(d)/2​=2log(d)T​. ■\blacksquare■

Here are Steps 3 to 5 checked on the same hostile run as before:

from math import exp, log, sqrt

d, T = 10, 2000
eta = sqrt(2 * log(d) / T)
w_t, ok, paid, totals = [1.0] * d, True, 0.0, [0.0] * d
for t in range(T):
    Z = sum(w_t)
    w = [wi / Z for wi in w_t]
    trusted = sorted(range(d), key=lambda i: -w[i])[:d // 2]
    v = [1.0 if i in trusted else 0.0 for i in range(d)]
    wv = sum(wi * vi for wi, vi in zip(w, v))
    w_t = [wi * exp(-eta * vi) for wi, vi in zip(w_t, v)]
    ok &= log(sum(w_t) / Z) <= -eta * wv + eta ** 2 / 2
    paid += wv
    totals = [s + vi for s, vi in zip(totals, v)]
log_Z = log(sum(w_t))
print(ok, round(log_Z - log(d), 2),
      round(-eta * paid + T * eta ** 2 / 2, 2))
print(round(log_Z, 2), round(-eta * min(totals), 2))

It prints True -47.99 -46.26 and -45.68 -47.99. Step 3 held on every round (True); the telescoped total log⁡ZT+1−log⁡d=−47.99\log Z_{T+1} - \log d = -47.99logZT+1​−logd=−47.99 sits below Step 4’s right side, −46.26-46.26−46.26; and log⁡ZT+1=−45.68\log Z_{T+1} = -45.68logZT+1​=−45.68 sits above Step 5’s floor, −47.99-47.99−47.99.

And the choice of η\etaη really does minimize the two-force bound:

from math import log, sqrt

d, T = 10, 2000
bound = lambda eta: log(d) / eta + eta * T / 2
etas = [k / 10_000 for k in range(1, 10_000)]
best = min(etas, key=bound)
print(best, round(bound(best), 2))
eta_star = sqrt(2 * log(d) / T)
print(round(eta_star, 4), round(sqrt(2 * log(d) * T), 2))

It prints 0.048 95.97 twice: a grid search over η\etaη finds the same minimum as the formula, at η≈0.048\eta \approx 0.048η≈0.048, with value about 96.

What if T≤2log⁡dT \le 2 \log dT≤2logd? Then 2log⁡(d) T≥T\sqrt{2 \log(d)\, T} \ge T2log(d)T​≥T, and the bound is true for free: no learner can pay more than TTT above anyone, since each round costs between 0 and 1. The condition only matters for the proof, not for the truth of the statement.

From experts to hypotheses

Now back to classification. Let H={h1,…,hd}\mathcal H = \{h_1, \dots, h_d\}H={h1​,…,hd​} be finite, and make each hypothesis an expert: expert iii advises hi(xt)h_i(x_t)hi​(xt​), and its cost is vt,i=∣hi(xt)−yt∣v_{t,i} = |h_i(x_t) - y_t|vt,i​=∣hi​(xt​)−yt​∣, 1 if it is wrong and 0 if it is right. The learner predicts the weighted vote, pt=∑iwi(t)hi(xt)p_t = \sum_i w_i^{(t)} h_i(x_t)pt​=∑i​wi(t)​hi​(xt​), as its probability of saying junk. For example, with weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 on three hypotheses that say junk, keep, junk, the learner says junk with probability 0.5+0.2=0.70.5 + 0.2 = 0.70.5+0.2=0.7.

Is the learner’s expected mistake ∣pt−yt∣|p_t - y_t|∣pt​−yt​∣ the same as Weighted-Majority’s cost ⟨w(t),vt⟩\langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle⟨w(t),vt​⟩? It is, and the reason is a sign argument:

∣pt−yt∣=∣∑iwi(t)(hi(xt)−yt)∣=∑iwi(t)∣hi(xt)−yt∣=⟨w(t),vt⟩.|p_t - y_t| = \Big| \sum_i w_i^{(t)} \big( h_i(x_t) - y_t \big) \Big| = \sum_i w_i^{(t)} \big| h_i(x_t) - y_t \big| = \langle \mathbf w^{(t)}, \mathbf v_t \rangle.∣pt​−yt​∣=​i∑​wi(t)​(hi​(xt​)−yt​)​=i∑​wi(t)​​hi​(xt​)−yt​​=⟨w(t),vt​⟩.

The first equality uses ∑iwi(t)=1\sum_i w_i^{(t)} = 1∑i​wi(t)​=1 to write yt=∑iwi(t)yty_t = \sum_i w_i^{(t)} y_tyt​=∑i​wi(t)​yt​. For the second: if yt=1y_t = 1yt​=1, every hi(xt)−yth_i(x_t) - y_thi​(xt​)−yt​ is 0 or −1-1−1, all of one sign; if yt=0y_t = 0yt​=0, every one is 0 or +1+1+1. The absolute value of a sum of terms of one sign is the sum of their absolute values. In words: because all the hypotheses err in the same direction, the vote’s distance from the label is exactly the weighted fraction of hypotheses that are wrong. In the example, if the message is keep, ∣0.7−0∣=0.7|0.7 - 0| = 0.7∣0.7−0∣=0.7, and the hypotheses that are wrong (the two saying junk) carry weight 0.5+0.2=0.70.5 + 0.2 = 0.70.5+0.2=0.7.

import random

rng = random.Random(3)
for trial in range(10_000):
    d = rng.randint(1, 6)
    w = [rng.random() for _ in range(d)]
    w = [wi / sum(w) for wi in w]
    h = [rng.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(d)]
    y = rng.randint(0, 1)
    p = sum(wi * hi for wi, hi in zip(w, h))
    rhs = sum(wi * abs(hi - y) for wi, hi in zip(w, h))
    assert abs(abs(p - y) - rhs) < 1e-12
print("identity holds in 10,000 random checks")

It prints identity holds in 10,000 random checks. And ∑tvt,i\sum_t v_{t,i}∑t​vt,i​ is just the number of mistakes of hih_ihi​. So Weighted-Majority’s theorem becomes, directly:

Corollary (finite classes). For a finite H\mathcal HH and T>2log⁡∣H∣T > 2 \log |\mathcal H|T>2log∣H∣, the weighted vote learner has, on every sequence,

∑t=1T∣pt−yt∣−min⁡h∈H∑t=1T∣h(xt)−yt∣≤2log⁡(∣H∣) T.\sum_{t=1}^T |p_t - y_t| - \min_{h \in \mathcal H} \sum_{t=1}^T |h(x_t) - y_t| \le \sqrt{2 \log(|\mathcal H|) \, T}.t=1∑T​∣pt​−yt​∣−h∈Hmin​t=1∑T​∣h(xt​)−yt​∣≤2log(∣H∣)T​.

In plain words: with a finite class, the randomized filter’s expected mistakes exceed those of the best hypothesis in hindsight by at most 2log⁡(∣H∣) T\sqrt{2 \log(|\mathcal H|)\, T}2log(∣H∣)T​. For lesson 1’s ten one-feature hypotheses over 2,000 messages, that is the 96 we computed: under 5% extra mistakes per round, against the worst spammers.

What about an infinite class? The rogue-sender class from earlier has one hypothesis per possible sender address, and there are infinitely many addresses, so log⁡∣H∣=∞\log |\mathcal H| = \inftylog∣H∣=∞. But its Littlestone dimension is 1. Can we build a finite set of experts that, on whatever messages arrive, includes one that behaves exactly like the best hypothesis?

Here is the idea in words. SOA, run on messages labelled by some hhh, makes at most L=Ldim(H)L = \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)L=Ldim(H) mistakes. If you knew on which rounds it would make them, you could reproduce hhh exactly: follow SOA’s guess, except flip it on those rounds. You don’t know the rounds, so create one expert for every possible set of at most LLL rounds. One of them has the right set.

Expert(i_1, ..., i_L), for rounds i_1 < ... < i_L:
  V_1 ← H
  for t = 1, 2, ..., T:
    receive x_t
    for r in {0, 1}: V_t^(r) ← {h in V_t : h(x_t) = r}
    guess ← argmax over r of Ldim(V_t^(r))   (ties: 0)
    if t is one of i_1, ..., i_L: predict 1 − guess
    else: predict guess
    V_{t+1} ← V_t^(prediction)

Each expert only needs the messages so far, never the labels, so it can advise in real time.

Lemma (some expert copies each hypothesis). Let Ldim(H)<∞\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) < \inftyLdim(H)<∞ and fix any messages x1,…,xTx_1, \dots, x_Tx1​,…,xT​. For every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H there are L≤Ldim(H)L \le \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)L≤Ldim(H) and rounds i1<⋯<iLi_1 < \dots < i_Li1​<⋯<iL​ such that Expert(i1,…,iL)\mathrm{Expert}(i_1, \dots, i_L)Expert(i1​,…,iL​) predicts h(xt)h(x_t)h(xt​) on every round ttt.

Proof. Run SOA (with ties going to 0, as in the expert) on the sequence (x1,h(x1)),…,(xT,h(xT))(x_1, h(x_1)), \dots, (x_T, h(x_T))(x1​,h(x1​)),…,(xT​,h(xT​)). It is realizable, labelled by hhh, so SOA makes at most Ldim(H)\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)Ldim(H) mistakes; let LLL be their number and i1,…,iLi_1, \dots, i_Li1​,…,iL​ the rounds where they happen. Now compare SOA with Expert(i1,…,iL)\mathrm{Expert}(i_1, \dots, i_L)Expert(i1​,…,iL​), round by round. Suppose both have the same version space at the start of round ttt (true at t=1t = 1t=1). They then compute the same guess. On a round in the list, SOA’s guess was wrong, so h(xt)=1−guessh(x_t) = 1 - \text{guess}h(xt​)=1−guess, which is what the expert predicts; on any other round, SOA’s guess was right, so h(xt)=guessh(x_t) = \text{guess}h(xt​)=guess, which again is what the expert predicts. Either way the expert predicts h(xt)h(x_t)h(xt​), and both then keep Vt(h(xt))V_t^{(h(x_t))}Vt(h(xt​))​, so the version spaces agree at round t+1t + 1t+1 too. By induction, the expert predicts h(xt)h(x_t)h(xt​) on every round. ■\blacksquare■

In plain words: for any hypothesis, one of the experts is a perfect copy of it on the messages that actually arrived. Here is the construction on H1\mathcal H_1H1​, for six messages: for each of the four hypotheses, find SOA’s mistake rounds, then check that the expert with those rounds reproduces the hypothesis.

from functools import lru_cache
from itertools import product

X = ["".join(b) for b in product("01", repeat=4)]
H = frozenset(tuple(int(x[k]) for x in X) for k in range(4))
part = lambda V, i, r: frozenset(h for h in V if h[i] == r)

@lru_cache(None)
def ldim(V):
    splits = [(part(V, i, 0), part(V, i, 1)) for i in range(16)]
    return -1 if not V else max([1 + min(map(ldim, s))
                                 for s in splits if all(s)],
                                default=0)

def run(xs, flips=(), labels=None):
    V, out = H, []
    for t, x in enumerate(xs, 1):
        i = X.index(x)
        guess = int(ldim(part(V, i, 1)) > ldim(part(V, i, 0)))
        flip = t in flips
        out.append(labels[t - 1] if labels else guess ^ flip)
        flips = flips if out[-1] == guess else (*flips, t)
        V = part(V, i, out[-1])
    return out, flips

xs = ["1100", "0011", "1010", "0110", "1111", "0001"]
for h in sorted(H):
    labels = [h[X.index(x)] for x in xs]
    flips = run(xs, labels=labels)[1]
    print(flips, run(xs, flips)[0] == labels)

It prints (1, 3) True, (1,) True, (3,) True and () True: the four hypotheses need flips at rounds {1, 3}, {1}, {3} and none, never more than Ldim(H1)=2\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H_1) = 2Ldim(H1​)=2 flips, and each expert copies its hypothesis exactly. The function run is SOA when given labels (it records where its guess was wrong) and the expert when given flips.

How many experts is that? One for each set of at most L=Ldim(H)L = \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)L=Ldim(H) rounds out of TTT:

d=∑k=0L(Tk)≤(eTL)L(1≤L≤T).d = \sum_{k=0}^{L} \binom{T}{k} \le \left( \frac{eT}{L} \right)^L \quad (1 \le L \le T).d=k=0∑L​(kT​)≤(LeT​)L(1≤L≤T).
  • (Tk)\binom{T}{k}(kT​) (“TTT choose kkk”) is the number of ways to pick kkk rounds out of TTT.
  • The sum counts all the sets of size 0,1,…,L0, 1, \dots, L0,1,…,L.
  • The inequality is the polynomial bound from Sauer’s lemma in lesson 6, with TTT in place of mmm and LLL in place of ddd.

In plain words: the number of experts grows only polynomially in TTT, like TLT^LTL, not exponentially. For the rogue sender, L=1L = 1L=1, and over T=10,000T = 10{,}000T=10,000 rounds there are 1+10,000=10,0011 + 10{,}000 = 10{,}0011+10,000=10,001 experts, below e⋅10,000≈27,183e \cdot 10{,}000 \approx 27{,}183e⋅10,000≈27,183. So log⁡d≤Llog⁡(eT/L)≤Llog⁡(eT)\log d \le L \log(eT/L) \le L \log(eT)logd≤Llog(eT/L)≤Llog(eT). Now run Weighted-Majority over these experts. For any h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H, the lemma gives an expert that copies hhh on the messages that arrived, so the best expert made at most as many mistakes as hhh, and a regret bound against the best expert is a regret bound against hhh: 2Llog⁡(eT) T\sqrt{2 L \log(eT)\, T}2Llog(eT)T​.

from math import comb, e, log, sqrt

T, L = 10_000, 1
experts = sum(comb(T, k) for k in range(L + 1))
print(experts, round((e * T / L) ** L))
regret = sqrt(2 * log(experts) * T)
print(round(regret, 1), round(regret / T, 4))
print(round(sqrt(2 * L * log(e * T) * T), 1))

It prints 10001 27183, then 429.2 0.0429 (the regret bound with the exact expert count, about 4.3% of the rounds), then 451.9 (the slightly looser 2Llog⁡(eT) T\sqrt{2L\log(eT)\,T}2Llog(eT)T​). An infinite class, an adversary, and still a guarantee.

Theorem (online learnability with regret). For every class H\mathcal HH there is an online learner whose predictions are probabilities pt∈[0,1]p_t \in [0, 1]pt​∈[0,1] and that satisfies, for every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H and every sequence,

∑t=1T∣pt−yt∣−∑t=1T∣h(xt)−yt∣≤2min⁡{log⁡∣H∣,  Ldim(H)log⁡(eT)} T.\sum_{t=1}^T |p_t - y_t| - \sum_{t=1}^T |h(x_t) - y_t| \le \sqrt{2 \min\{\log |\mathcal H|, \; \mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H) \log(eT)\} \, T}.t=1∑T​∣pt​−yt​∣−t=1∑T​∣h(xt​)−yt​∣≤2min{log∣H∣,Ldim(H)log(eT)}T​.

Moreover, no learner can guarantee an expected regret smaller than a constant times Ldim(H) T\sqrt{\mathrm{Ldim}(\mathcal H)\, T}Ldim(H)T​.

In plain words: with a coin, every class of finite Littlestone dimension can be learned online against any sequence, with regret growing like T\sqrt TT​; and that is the best possible rate. For the rogue sender, log⁡∣H∣=∞\log |\mathcal H| = \inftylog∣H∣=∞, so the minimum picks 1⋅log⁡(e⋅10,000)≈10.21 \cdot \log(e \cdot 10{,}000) \approx 10.21⋅log(e⋅10,000)≈10.2, and over 10,000 rounds the bound is the 451.9 printed above. The upper bound is the two constructions above: the finite one, and the Littlestone experts (when Ldim=0\mathrm{Ldim} = 0Ldim=0, the class has a single behaviour and the bound is 0). We prove the upper bound only; the matching lower bound is a research result we state without proof. So the Littlestone dimension decides learnability online in both settings, realizable and not, just as the VC dimension did for the batch world in lesson 6.

Online convex optimization

Weighted-Majority needs a list of experts, which for big classes is a big list. In lessons 12 and 14 you met a different way to make learning tractable: convex losses, minimized by stepping against a subgradient. Does that survive an adversary? Yes, almost word for word.

The setting in words: each round, the learner commits to a weight vector, the adversary (adapting to everything so far) reveals an example, and the learner pays a loss that is convex in the vector, as in lesson 12, over a convex set of allowed vectors.

Online convex optimization. A hypothesis class H⊆Rn\mathcal H \subseteq \mathbb R^nH⊆Rn that is a convex set (we write nnn for the number of coordinates, since ddd already counts experts), a domain ZZZ of examples, and a loss ℓ:H×Z→R\ell : \mathcal H \times Z \to \mathbb Rℓ:H×Z→R with ℓ(⋅,z)\ell(\cdot, z)ℓ(⋅,z) convex for every zzz. For t=1,…,Tt = 1, \dots, Tt=1,…,T: the learner announces w(t)∈H\mathbf w^{(t)} \in \mathcal Hw(t)∈H, the environment answers with zt∈Zz_t \in Zzt​∈Z, and the learner pays ℓ(w(t),zt)\ell(\mathbf w^{(t)}, z_t)ℓ(w(t),zt​).

Regret is measured against any fixed vector w⋆\mathbf w^\starw⋆:

RegretA(w⋆,T)=∑t=1Tℓ(w(t),zt)−∑t=1Tℓ(w⋆,zt),RegretA(H,T)=sup⁡w⋆∈HRegretA(w⋆,T).\mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathbf w^\star, T) = \sum_{t=1}^T \ell(\mathbf w^{(t)}, z_t) - \sum_{t=1}^T \ell(\mathbf w^\star, z_t), \qquad \mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathcal H, T) = \sup_{\mathbf w^\star \in \mathcal H} \mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathbf w^\star, T).RegretA​(w⋆,T)=t=1∑T​ℓ(w(t),zt​)−t=1∑T​ℓ(w⋆,zt​),RegretA​(H,T)=w⋆∈Hsup​RegretA​(w⋆,T).
  • The first sum is the learner’s total loss with its changing vectors; the second is the total loss of the single vector w⋆\mathbf w^\starw⋆, held fixed, on the same examples.
  • sup⁡w⋆∈H\sup_{\mathbf w^\star \in \mathcal H}supw⋆∈H​ picks the comparison vector that makes the learner look worst: the best fixed vector in hindsight.

In plain words: the regret is how much more loss the learner paid than the best single weight vector it could have used throughout. For example, if over 100 rounds the learner pays 60 and the best fixed vector would have paid 52, the regret against it is 8.

The learner is Online Gradient Descent: lesson 14’s gradient descent with projection, run on the losses as they arrive. Recall from lesson 14 that a subgradient v\mathbf vv of a convex fff at w\mathbf ww is the slope of a supporting plane: f(u)≥f(w)+⟨u−w,v⟩f(\mathbf u) \ge f(\mathbf w) + \langle \mathbf u - \mathbf w, \mathbf v \ranglef(u)≥f(w)+⟨u−w,v⟩ for every u\mathbf uu; that fff is ρ\rhoρ-Lipschitz exactly when every subgradient has norm at most ρ\rhoρ; and the projection lemma: projecting onto a convex set never increases the distance to any point of the set.

OnlineGradientDescent(η):
  w^(1) ← 0
  for t = 1, 2, ..., T:
    predict w^(t)
    receive z_t; let f_t(w) = ℓ(w, z_t)
    choose a subgradient v_t of f_t at w^(t)
    w^(t+½) ← w^(t) − η v_t
    w^(t+1) ← the point of H closest to w^(t+½)

The half step moves against the subgradient, and the projection pulls the vector back into H\mathcal HH if it stepped outside.

[diagram:ogd: built on the lesson page]

Theorem (Online Gradient Descent’s regret). For every w⋆∈H\mathbf w^\star \in \mathcal Hw⋆∈H,

RegretA(w⋆,T)≤∥w⋆∥22η+η2∑t=1T∥vt∥2.\mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathbf w^\star, T) \le \frac{\|\mathbf w^\star\|^2}{2\eta} + \frac{\eta}{2} \sum_{t=1}^T \|\mathbf v_t\|^2.RegretA​(w⋆,T)≤2η∥w⋆∥2​+2η​t=1∑T​∥vt​∥2.

If every ftf_tft​ is ρ\rhoρ-Lipschitz and η=1/T\eta = 1/\sqrt Tη=1/T​, then RegretA(w⋆,T)≤12(∥w⋆∥2+ρ2)T\mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathbf w^\star, T) \le \frac12 (\|\mathbf w^\star\|^2 + \rho^2) \sqrt TRegretA​(w⋆,T)≤21​(∥w⋆∥2+ρ2)T​. If moreover every vector in H\mathcal HH has norm at most BBB and η=B/(ρT)\eta = B/(\rho \sqrt T)η=B/(ρT​), then RegretA(H,T)≤BρT\mathrm{Regret}_A(\mathcal H, T) \le B \rho \sqrt TRegretA​(H,T)≤BρT​.

  • ∥w⋆∥\|\mathbf w^\star\|∥w⋆∥ is the length of the comparison vector: how far it is from the starting point 0\mathbf 00.
  • ∥vt∥2\|\mathbf v_t\|^2∥vt​∥2 is the squared length of the step direction on round ttt.
  • The two terms are lesson 14’s two forces again: a timid step size pays for the distance to cover, and a bold one pays for the size of its steps.

In plain words: against any sequence of convex losses, Online Gradient Descent pays at most BρTB\rho\sqrt TBρT​ more than the best fixed vector, the same bound gradient descent had in lesson 14, now with no distribution at all. With B=1B = 1B=1, ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1 and T=10,000T = 10{,}000T=10,000 rounds, the regret is at most 100, one hundredth of a loss per round.

Proof. Fix w⋆∈H\mathbf w^\star \in \mathcal Hw⋆∈H. Track the squared distance to it, ∥w(t)−w⋆∥2\|\mathbf w^{(t)} - \mathbf w^\star\|^2∥w(t)−w⋆∥2, and see how much one round changes it. Add and subtract the half step:
